newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Apartheid defence minister to help truth body.
newsitem.headline: Apartheid defence minister to help truth body.

text.p: Former defence minister General Magnus Malan volunteered on Wednesday to cooperate with South Africa's truth commission in what the commission called a breakthrough in efforts to uncover the crimes of apartheid.
Archbishop Desmond Tutu, chairman of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, said in a statement he had an hour- long meeting with Malan in Cape Town at the general's request.
"He informed me that he is willing to testify before the commission to help us obtain a complete picture of the role which the former South African Defence Force played," Tutu said.
"I welcome very warmly General Malan's initiative," he said, adding that Malan would probably testify in public early next month.
Malan, 67, became chief of the defence force in 1976, the year that widespread student riots marked the start of the intensification of guerrilla war against the white-led government.

He served as defence minister for most of the 1980s and was seen as a protege of the then president, P.W. Botha, who struggled to maintain apartheid in the face of pressure from abroad and increasing protests at home.
Tutu told a news conference after meeting Malan that the general's decision to cooperate could pave the way for many soldiers who served under him to also come forward.
"He said he believed in reconciliation and thought that he wanted to make his contribution... He wanted to be able to give an indication of how things happened (in the military)," Tutu said.
"He said we could put any questions to him...Off his own bat he was saying no area was taboo."
Tutu's deputy chairman Alec Boraine called Malan's decision a breakthrough because it indicated a widening acceptance of the work of the commission. "It is a very major step forward," Boraine said.
Malan and 19 others, including several fellow defence force generals, were acquitted last year on murder charges arising from the killing of 13 blacks in the KwaZulu-Natal settlement of KwaMakutha.

The prosecution failed during the trial to prove that the defence force was directly responsible for the killing, one of scores of massacres during a decade of feuding between President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress and the Inkatha Freedom Party of Mangosuthu Buthelezi.

Other court trials and testimony to the truth commission have produced evidence that some units of the defence force, including special forces and military intelligence, were deeply involved in extra-judicial killings during the apartheid race war.

The truth commission's mandate is to heal the wounds of apartheid by exposing as much as possible of the crimes and human rights abuses committed by both sides of the apartheid divide. It has powers to give amnesty for perpetrators who confess.
